clue.text: Not in suitable attire

parts.note: someone not in is out
fit means suitable or appropriate

explanation.surface: Someone turns up badly dressed for the occasion.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Not in suitable attire' reads as one phrase, but it splits into two pieces and a one-word definition at the end.
explanation.definitionFit: An outfit is a set of clothes worn together, which is what attire means.

clue.text: University can come up to an accepted standard

parts.note: U is the standard abbreviation for university

indicators.note: in a down entry, coming up means the word is read from the bottom upwards

parts.note: a tin is a can

explanation.surface: A university manages to reach a recognised level of quality.
explanation.walkthrough: 'can' looks like a verb meaning 'is able to', but it is the noun, a tin.
explanation.definitionFit: A unit is a fixed quantity agreed upon for measuring, such as the metre or kilogram.

clue.text: No paying guest has this room above water

definitions.text: No paying guest has this room above water

parts.note: surface reading: a guest who does not pay for meals and lodging
setter's reading: the clearance on a ship between waterline and deck

explanation.walkthrough: A guest who pays nothing gets free board, but 'room' here is space, the height of a ship's side above the water.
explanation.definitionFit: Freeboard is the nautical term for the distance between the waterline and the upper deck of a vessel.

clue.text: Ill-fated US soldier trapped in overturned wagon

indicators.note: something trapped in something else sits inside it, enclosed on both sides
a vehicle overturned is upside down, so in a down entry its word is read upwards

parts.note: a cart is a simple wagon
GI is the familiar term for an American soldier

explanation.surface: An unlucky American soldier is pinned under a wagon that has rolled over.
explanation.definitionFit: Something tragic ends in disaster or suffering, so it is doomed or unlucky in its fate.

clue.text: Obviously not Oxbridge material

parts.note: surface reading: a student not clever enough for Oxford or Cambridge
setter's reading: the building material of newer universities, as opposed to ancient stone

explanation.walkthrough: Redbrick universities are the English civic universities founded in the Victorian era, named for their brick buildings, contrasted with ancient Oxford and Cambridge.
explanation.definitionFit: The term describes British universities built in brick in industrial cities, outside the older Oxbridge pair.

clue.text: It may enable fighters to make a comeback

definitions.text: It may enable fighters to make a comeback

parts.note: surface reading: boxers or teams recovering after losing ground
setter's reading: troops at the back holding off the enemy while the army retreats

explanation.walkthrough: A comeback sounds like a recovery, but here it means literally coming back, a retreat covered by the soldiers at the rear.
explanation.definitionFit: A rearguard action is fighting by the rear troops to protect an army as it withdraws.

clue.text: Action by head required for new title

definitions.note: a descriptive definition: what the document is needed for

parts.note: a deed is an act or action
poll is an old word for the head, as in poll tax

explanation.surface: A boss must take some step before someone can be given a new job title.
explanation.walkthrough: A deed poll is the British legal document used to change one's name.
explanation.definitionFit: Changing a surname or title officially in Britain requires signing this legal declaration, so it is what a new name needs.

clue.text: With spirit, a sailor gets up to dance

parts.note: rum is a spirit, a strong liquor

indicators.note: getting up means rising, so in a down entry the word reads from bottom to top

parts.note: AB, able seaman, is a sailor

explanation.surface: A sailor, fortified by drink, rises to take a turn on the dance floor.
explanation.definitionFit: The rumba is a Cuban ballroom dance with swaying hip movements.

clue.text: Hardcastle is converted in religious places

indicators.note: converted means changed into another form, so the letters are rearranged

parts.note: taken as written; it sounds like a person's surname

explanation.surface: Someone named Hardcastle finds religion in churches.
explanation.walkthrough: 'converted' fits the religious surface perfectly, which hides that it signals rearrangement.
explanation.definitionFit: Cathedrals are the principal churches of dioceses, so they are places of worship.

clue.text: Widely shown film of American disaster

indicators.note: a disaster wrecks things, leaving the letters in ruins to be rebuilt

parts.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: A Hollywood disaster movie is screened everywhere.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Widely shown' suggests a film in every cinema; it really means shown on a wide screen.
explanation.definitionFit: Cinerama was a widescreen projection process using three cameras, so its films were literally shown wide.

clue.text: It is displayed when mien changes extremely threateningly

definitions.text: It is displayed when mien changes extremely threateningly

indicators.note: a word that changes alters its form, so its letters are shuffled

parts.note: taken as written; mien is a person's look or bearing

indicators.note: the extremes of a word are its two ends, so only first and last letters count

parts.note: the first and last letters of the word

explanation.surface: Hostility shows when someone's expression turns menacing.
explanation.walkthrough: The whole clue is both the definition and the wordplay: hostility is what shows when a face turns threatening.
explanation.definitionFit: Enmity is hostility or ill will, the feeling revealed by a sudden menacing look.

clue.text: He may have to make several calls before getting the contract

definitions.text: He may have to make several calls before getting the contract

parts.words: make several calls before getting the contract
parts.note: surface reading: a salesman phoning round before winning a business deal
setter's reading: a card player bidding in an auction for the right to play a hand

explanation.walkthrough: In the card game bridge, bids are called 'calls' and the final bid is 'the contract'.
explanation.definitionFit: A participant at the bridge table bids during the auction until one side wins the contract to play.

clue.text: Secure telephone provided for the explosives expert

parts.note: safe means secure, out of danger
blower is British slang for the telephone

explanation.surface: An encrypted phone line is supplied to a bomb disposal specialist.
explanation.walkthrough: A safeblower is a criminal who blows open safes with explosives.
explanation.definitionFit: A safe-blower cracks strongboxes using explosive charges, making the thief a specialist with explosives.

clue.text: Senile and repetitive state

wordplay.note: GA, the abbreviation for the US state of Georgia, repeated

explanation.surface: An old person grows doddery and says the same things over and over.
explanation.walkthrough: 'repetitive state' sounds like a mental condition, but it is a US state abbreviation written twice.
explanation.definitionFit: Gaga is an informal word for confused or doddering through old age.

clue.text: Go really wild with a symbolic tale

indicators.note: letters running wild are out of control and out of order

parts.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: An instruction to let loose with an imaginative fable.
explanation.definitionFit: An allegory is a story whose characters and events stand for deeper moral or political meanings.

clue.text: Provisionally supply one seeking earthly riches

definitions.text: Provisionally supply one seeking earthly riches

parts.note: surface reading: to fund someone for the time being
setter's reading: to give food to a gold prospector digging in the ground

explanation.walkthrough: 'Provisionally' sounds like 'temporarily' but means 'with provisions', and 'earthly riches' are minerals dug from the earth.
explanation.definitionFit: To grubstake is to furnish a prospector with food and equipment in return for a share of any find.

clue.text: Spoils Worcestershire opener's time at the crease

indicators.note: an opener comes first, so only the initial letter of the county is wanted

parts.note: the county's first letter
in cricket, the crease is where the batsman stands, and an innings is a turn at batting

explanation.surface: A Worcestershire opening batsman throws away his turn at bat.
explanation.walkthrough: The cricket surface makes 'Spoils' look like a verb (ruins), but it is the noun for gains; Worcestershire is an English county with a cricket team.
explanation.definitionFit: Winnings are money or prizes gained, just as spoils are the booty taken by victors.

clue.text: It's a blow that has to be faced

definitions.text: It's a blow that has to be faced

parts.words: a blow that has to be faced
parts.note: surface reading: a setback or misfortune one must confront
setter's reading: a gust blowing straight into one's face

explanation.walkthrough: 'Blow' suggests a misfortune, but it is literally the wind blowing, and 'faced' is meant physically.
explanation.definitionFit: A headwind blows directly against the direction of travel, so walkers or pilots must move straight into it.

clue.text: Fruit, nothing like a peach we hear

indicators.note: what we hear is a spoken word, so the spelling differs from the sound

parts.note: a peach is an attractive person, so the opposite is unattractive

explanation.surface: A fruit that looks nothing like a peach.
explanation.walkthrough: The ugli is a wrinkled Jamaican citrus fruit named for its appearance; 'a peach' in slang is a beauty.
explanation.definitionFit: The ugli is a hybrid citrus, a cross of grapefruit and tangerine, so it is a fruit.

clue.text: The boring bits of exercises

definitions.meaning: first meaning: tools that bore holes
second meaning: repeated practice routines, as in military training

explanation.surface: The tedious parts of a workout.
explanation.walkthrough: 'boring' looks like 'dull', but it means making holes.
explanation.definitionFit: Drill bits bore holes, and drills are repetitive training routines such as parade-ground practice.

clue.text: They are suited for indoor games

definitions.text: They are suited for indoor games

parts.note: surface reading: people dressed appropriately for an activity
setter's reading: items divided into hearts, clubs, diamonds and spades for parlour games

explanation.walkthrough: 'suited' sounds like 'appropriate' or 'dressed', but a pack is divided into four suits.
explanation.definitionFit: A standard pack is split into four suits and used for games such as bridge, poker and rummy.

clue.text: Bound to pull together

parts.note: surface reading: certain to cooperate as a team
setter's reading: oxen tied by a wooden crossbar so they haul in tandem

explanation.walkthrough: 'Bound to' looks like 'certain to', but it means literally tied, like a pair of oxen.
explanation.definitionFit: Animals that are yoked are joined at the neck by a wooden frame so they haul a load as a pair.

clue.text: Drop of moisture round bearing is not good

indicators.note: going round something means encircling it, holding it inside

parts.note: bad is the opposite of good
east is a compass bearing, abbreviated E

explanation.surface: Damp around a mechanical bearing is a problem.
explanation.walkthrough: 'bearing' suggests a machine part, but it is a compass direction.
explanation.definitionFit: A bead is a small round drop of liquid, such as a bead of sweat.

clue.text: Come to a potentially weak point

parts.note: taken as written

indicators.note: potentially means in a possible form, so the word could be rearranged into another

parts.note: taken as written
a compass point, north

explanation.surface: Arriving at a spot that might prove vulnerable.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Come to' reads as 'arrive at', but it means regain consciousness.
explanation.definitionFit: To come to is to recover consciousness, and to awaken is to stop sleeping or rouse oneself.

clue.text: Doomed to have poor health?

definitions.meaning: second meaning, read literally: fated to be sick

explanation.walkthrough: The question mark flags the literal reading: one whose fate is to be unwell.
explanation.definitionFit: Ill-fated means destined to fail or meet misfortune, which is what doomed means.

clue.text: Unusually strained exchanges

indicators.note: unusually means not in the normal way, so the letters fall in an odd order

parts.note: taken as written

explanation.walkthrough: 'exchanges' suggests words between people, but it is the verb for handing over an old item as part-payment.
explanation.definitionFit: To trade in an old car is to give it up in part exchange for a new one.

clue.text: Stable companion?

definitions.meaning: second meaning: a regular boyfriend or girlfriend

explanation.walkthrough: Read together, 'Stable companion' sounds like a horse's stablemate; the two words are separate meanings.
explanation.definitionFit: Steady means firm and unshakeable, and a steady is a regular romantic partner.
